name: Victor Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm a backend developer at a company that makes route-planning software for delivery firms, so my code decides which van goes down which street. I'm in by half nine, check overnight alerts, then stand-up with my team of six. Most of the day I'm building or fixing the services that crunch the routes, and I have an AI coding assistant open the whole time, like a very fast junior who never gets tired.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the puzzle side: a driver in a real town finishes forty minutes earlier because of something I shipped. What wears me out is the on-call week, when the phone buzzes at 3am because a depot's routes didn't load. I'm 27, I live with my partner Iris, who teaches at a primary school, and we've got a good chunk saved, so the job isn't a money worry right now. It's more that I want it to mean something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already half say in the team chat: the tools are handy, the hype was oversold, and the boring parts of coding got a bit faster. Online I'd probably post something smug about how the people who said all developers were finished got it wrong. I'd also say the savings went to the shareholders, not to shorter weeks for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life stays about the same, which is fine. I already use the assistant for tests and boilerplate, the repetitive code you write a hundred times, so a plateau just locks in what I've got. I'd be a little disappointed, because I enjoy pushing the tools, but my job and pay would be safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at work and keep using the assistant where it helps. I'd put more energy into the tech workers' group a few of us started, because a calm market is when you can actually organise. Money-wise, I'd keep putting about 800 a month into savings and maybe start thinking about a flat with Iris.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relief, with a small itch of boredom. It's nice to picture a future where the ground isn't moving under everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the tech workers' group. What would you actually push for in a world like this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Clear rules on on-call pay, for a start, because right now a 3am call is just part of the salary. And a say in how the AI tools get used, so they don't become a way to count our keystrokes. My mate Dev (a developer on my team) jokes that the assistant is the only colleague who never complains, and that's exactly the attitude I'd want to push back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Iris, what would this picture mean for her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For Iris it would mean nothing much changes either, which for a teacher means still too many kids per class and not enough pay. If AI plateaus, I'd want the time it does save in offices to be used to fund schools properly. A plateau doesn't fix a classroom with thirty-two kids and one tired teacher.

say: The tools are **handy**, but the hype was **oversold** and coding just got a bit faster.
The time AI saved went to **shareholders**, not to **shorter weeks** for workers.
think: My **job** and pay stay safe, and the assistant keeps doing the **boring parts**.
I'd be a little **disappointed**, because I enjoy pushing the tools further.
do: Keep using the **AI assistant** for tests and repetitive code at work.
Put more energy into the **tech workers' group** while the market is calm.
Keep saving about **800 a month** and start looking at a flat with Iris.
feel: **Relief** that the ground stops moving, with a small itch of **boredom**.
S0.quote: A plateau doesn't fix a classroom with thirty-two kids and one tired teacher.
fieldNote: Already uses AI all day, so a plateau changes **almost nothing** in his own work.
His worry points outward, to **Iris's school** and workers' rights, not to his own pay.
Sees a calm market as the right time to **organise** colleagues.

steps.text: Keep using the coding assistant for tests and repetitive code
Push the tech workers' group for paid on-call and AI-use rules
Keep saving 800 a month toward a flat with Iris

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is the moment to get good at the tools, not to hide from them. With friends I'd be more political: if code gets cheaper to write, the people writing it deserve a share of what that saves. Online I'd probably share every story about a firm cutting a junior team and calling it efficiency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be one of the people who comes out fine, at least for a while. I'm already the person on my team who shows others how to get the assistant to write decent tests. The ones I'd worry about are the juniors and the testers, because their work is exactly what the tools eat first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first few months I'd ask my lead to let me own how our team uses AI, so I'm the person setting the rules rather than following them. I'd take a short course on running AI models inside our own systems, which my company would probably pay for. And I'd push the workers' group to ask for a written promise that no one gets cut just because a tool sped them up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, honestly, because I can see the gap opening between people like me and people like our tester Ruth (a colleague on my team). I feel lucky and a bit guilty about feeling lucky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Ruth's work is what the tools eat first. What would you actually say to Ruth?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Ruth to sit with me on Thursdays and learn to check what the AI writes, because checking is the part that won't vanish soon. I'd also tell Ruth to join the group, so she isn't alone if the company comes for her role. Ruth has been there six years and knows every weird customer bug by heart, which the tools don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're in a strong position and you'd still push for promises from the company. Isn't that a bit at odds with doing well out of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but I don't think so. Doing well out of a change doesn't mean I have to pretend it's fair to everyone. If my team keeps its jobs because I made a fuss, that's worth more to me than a bonus.

say: This is the time to **get good** at the tools, not hide from them.
If code gets cheaper, the people writing it deserve a **share** of the savings.
think: I'm likely to **come out fine** for a while, because I already teach the tools.
**Juniors and testers** are most at risk, since the tools eat their work first.
do: Ask his lead to let him own the team's **AI rules** within the first months.
Take a **company-paid course** on running AI models inside their own systems.
Push the workers' group for a **written promise** against cuts from tool speed-ups.
feel: **Uneasy** at the gap opening between him and colleagues like Ruth.
Lucky, and a bit **guilty** about feeling lucky.
S1.quote: Doing well out of a change doesn't mean I have to pretend it's fair to everyone.
fieldNote: Expects his **own job** to hold, so the unease is about colleagues, not himself.
Wants to **set the rules** for AI on his team rather than follow them.
Combines eager tool use with **union-style** demands, and sees no conflict between them.

steps.text: Ask his lead to let him run the team's AI rules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say governments have to move now: tax the companies that own these systems and pay people while things settle. At work I'd stop pretending, and I'd say plainly that most of what we do will be done by AI by 2028. I think a lot of developers would be angry at me for saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job is gone, and fast. Route-planning code is exactly the kind of thinking work full AGI does better and cheaper, and two years is nothing. Being good with the tools buys me maybe a year as the person who runs them, and then the tools run themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd stop saving for a flat and keep the money liquid, because I wouldn't want to lock it into a mortgage on a job that won't last. I'd spend evenings on a part-time course in electrical work, because robots for hands-on jobs come about three years later, around 2031. And I'd go all in on the workers' group and on campaigning for some kind of basic income before the layoffs hit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, really. Not panicked, because we have money and Iris's job is safer than mine for a while, but I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which sums would you be doing at 3am?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How many months we could cover the rent on Iris's salary alone, which is about fourteen if we cut the holidays and the takeaway. Whether I could earn anything in the three years before robots arrive. And whether it's mad to train as an electrician for a job that robots will also do by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI more than almost anyone you know. Does that change how this feels?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes it worse, in a way, because I know exactly how good the tools already are. I've watched the assistant fix a bug in ten minutes that took me a whole afternoon last year. People who never use it can still believe it's hype.

say: Governments must **tax** the companies that own these systems and **pay people** through it.
I'd say plainly at work that most of our job is **done by AI** by 2028.
think: My **job is gone**, and fast, because route-planning code is exactly what AGI does.
Being good with the tools buys me maybe **one year** at most.
do: Stop saving for a flat and keep the **savings liquid** instead.
Start a part-time **electrical course** in the evenings, before robots arrive around 2031.
Campaign through the workers' group for a **basic income** before layoffs hit.
feel: **Alarmed** and lying awake doing sums, though not **panicked** with savings behind him.
S2.quote: I've watched the assistant fix a bug in ten minutes that took me a whole afternoon last year.
fieldNote: His **daily AI use** makes him more alarmed, not less, because he sees its speed.
Uses the **3-year robot gap** to plan a move into hands-on electrical work.
Counts on **Iris's salary** covering about fourteen months of rent.

steps.text: Pause the flat search and keep savings in cash
Enrol in an evening electrical course this year
Campaign with the workers' group for a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years and no excuse, so let's use them: retraining money, shorter weeks, a public fund that owns a slice of these AI systems. At work I'd say it more calmly than in the two-year one. People listen better when they aren't in shock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd still lose my developer job, probably around 2030 or 2031, but five years is long enough to land somewhere. I could do two or three good years as the person who brings AI into our company, earn well, and save hard. The question is where I jump to before the music stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd say yes to every AI project at work and ask for a pay rise to match, then save the extra, maybe 1,500 a month. I'd start an evening course in electrical installation by year two, so I'm qualified before the thinking jobs go and with three years before robots catch up. And I'd help the workers' group draft a proposal for retraining time paid by the company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy-anxious, which I prefer. Having a plan with dates on it makes the fear smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Iris think of you becoming an electrician?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Iris laughed first, because I can't hang a picture straight. Then Iris said her dad was an electrician for thirty years and never once worried about a computer taking his job. I think that's partly why the idea sticks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you're bringing AI into your own company, aren't you speeding up the thing you're worried about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a bit, and I'd feel that. But the company will do it with me or without me, and if it's me, I can at least make sure people get warning and training. Refusing to touch AI wouldn't save a single job on my team.

say: Five years means **no excuse**: fund retraining, **shorter weeks** and public ownership.
People listen better when they **aren't in shock**, so I'd say it calmly.
think: I'd still **lose the developer job**, probably around 2030 or 2031.
Five years is long enough to **land somewhere** if I jump in time.
do: Volunteer for every **AI project** at work and ask for a matching pay rise.
Save the extra, about **1,500 a month**, while the good years last.
Start an evening **electrical installation** course by year two.
feel: **Anxious**, but busy-anxious, and a plan with **dates** shrinks the fear.
S3.quote: Refusing to touch AI wouldn't save a single job on my team.
fieldNote: Plans to **ride the wave** for two or three years, then move to hands-on work.
Admits he'd speed up the change, and justifies it by **protecting colleagues**.
**Iris's father**, an electrician, makes the trade switch feel real to him.

steps.text: Volunteer for AI projects and ask for a pay rise
Save about 1,500 a month from the higher pay
Start an evening electrical installation course by year two
Help draft a paid-retraining proposal with the workers' group

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and wasting it would be a choice. I'd be the annoying one at parties telling people to start planning now. Online I'd push for the law to make companies fund retraining while they still need us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have a really good decade before the developer job goes, maybe the best-paid years I'll ever have. I'd be 37 in 2036, which is young enough to start again. What scares me more is whether the country handles it fairly, not whether I personally land on my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't panic-switch. I'd keep developing, get very good at running AI systems, and save hard toward a flat with Iris in the next three years. Around 2030 I'd start a proper electrical apprenticeship or something hands-on, so I'm qualified by the time thinking AI arrives and have three more years before robots. And I'd stay active in the workers' group the whole way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly anxious for the country and fairly steady for us. It's a strange mix, like watching a slow storm come in while you have a good roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a flat with Iris. Would you still buy one in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably yes, but a small one, and only with a mortgage Iris could carry on a teacher's salary alone. That's the rule we'd set. If my income vanishes in 2036, we keep the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got a decade and a plan. What would make you still anxious?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People I care about who aren't planning. My brother Luca works in a call centre, and Luca's job goes years before mine. Luca doesn't want to talk about it, and I can't retrain on Luca's behalf.

The law should make companies **fund retraining** while they still need us.
think: I'd have a **good decade** before the developer job goes, maybe my best-paid.
My bigger worry is whether the country handles it **fairly**.
do: Keep developing and get very good at **running AI systems**.
Buy a **small flat** only on a mortgage Iris could carry alone.
Start a **hands-on apprenticeship** around 2030, before thinking AI arrives.
feel: Anxious for the **country**, fairly steady for his own **household**.
S4.quote: My brother Luca works in a call centre, and Luca's job goes years before mine.
fieldNote: A decade lets him plan in **stages** rather than jump now.

His anxiety rests on his own job's **end date** and on his brother Luca.

steps.text: Learn to run and maintain AI systems at work
Buy a small flat on a mortgage Iris can carry

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years isn't enough time for anyone to retrain, and the government would still be arguing when the layoffs came. What would help is paid time to retrain, a basic income while people switch, and a law that says companies replacing staff with AI pay into a public fund.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets the money. Everyone asks what happens to the jobs, but the real question is who owns the machines that do them. If developers end up owning a slice of that, the whole picture looks different.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks what happens to the jobs, but the real question is who owns the machines that do them.
portrait: A **27-year-old** backend developer on route-planning software, living with **Iris**, a primary school teacher.
Uses an **AI assistant** all day and is the team's go-to person for it.
Progressive and pro-union, he helps run a small **tech workers' group** at his company.
Stays calm in the plateau, uneasy in steady change, and **alarmed** by AGI in two years.
Plans a staged move into **electrical work**, using the three-year gap before robots.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because two years leaves no time to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** time and a **basic income** while people switch jobs.
A law making firms that replace staff with AI pay into a **public fund**.
